column1: # The artifacts a scheduled run can re-fetch unattended, and how.
# NOT every pinned artifact. Most of the corpus is reachable only
# through a human step — a repository checked out at a pinned commit, a
# distribution package unpacked, an archive whose member is the thing
# that is pinned — and inventing a URL for those would produce a monitor
# that reported failures about its own guesses. A row here is a promise
# that one HTTP GET returns the pinned bytes after the stated
# normalization, and nothing else.
# The complement is the interesting half and the monitor reports it: an
# artifact with no row has no unattended refresh route, which is a fact
# about this corpus worth knowing rather than a gap to hide.
# WHY THE TRUST-DOMAIN VENDOR'S SEVEN COLLATERAL DOCUMENTS HAVE NO ROW,
# measured rather than assumed -- and it is not the reason previously
# supposed. The supposed reason was that three of those endpoints select
# the collateral with a platform-family query parameter, so there is no
# one URL for "the trusted-computing-base document". That is true and it
# is not an obstacle: a row pins ONE artifact, the family that artifact
# describes is a property of the PIN, and the parameter belongs in the
# URL. Two of the seven take no parameter at all.
# The real obstacle is that THE SERVICE RE-SIGNS ON A CADENCE FAR SHORTER
# THAN THE VALIDITY IT STATES. Three back-to-back requests return
# byte-identical answers, so it is not per-request; a request three hours
# later returns a document whose issue/this-update and next-update have
# both moved by that interval and whose substance has not -- same
# evaluation-data number, same levels, same statuses, same advisories,
# same revoked serials. Observed 2026-10-02: 17:13:18 then 20:14:40 on
# one endpoint, 17:26:12 then 20:26:15 on another, both to the second.
# A row here promises that one HTTP GET returns the pinned bytes. For
# these seven that promise is false within three hours of any pin, so the
# drift half would report all seven as drifted on EVERY run, for ever,
# and re-pinning would not quieten it. That is a worse version of the
# condition the capped horizon was introduced to remove: an alarm that
# has never once been silent cannot say that something changed.
# What a drift route for them would need, concretely, so this is a
# deferral and not a dead end: a SUBSTANCE digest beside the byte digest
# -- the document with its two timestamp members excluded -- pinned in
# the ledger and compared against the same projection of the response. A
# difference in THAT is the signal worth having, because it is how a
# platform's trusted-computing-base policy moves, and a corpus pinned to
# the previous one is testing a policy nobody runs. Their expiry is
# watched meanwhile, which is what the capped horizon is for.
# The root revocation list below is a different case and does have a row:
# it is served from the certificate host rather than the provisioning
# API, states a one-year validity, and re-fetched byte-identical three
# hours apart.
# normalize:
#   none      the response body IS the artifact
#   strip-cr  the response body with carriage returns removed. One
#             vendor serves its certificate chains CRLF and the others
#             LF; a Nim triple-quoted literal in an LF file cannot carry
#             the carriage returns, so the pin is of the stripped form.
#             Applying it to all three chains is deliberate — it is a
#             no-op on the two that are already LF, and a rule with an
#             exception is a rule somebody gets wrong.
# name
